text: The scientists who first describe a new kind of dinosaur get to name it. They must publish a careful description in a scientific journal. They also pick one particular [[fossil|fossil]] to be the "name-bearer", the specimen that the name will always belong to.

Names follow an international rule book. Every [[species|species]] gets two parts, like Tyrannosaurus rex or Rajasaurus narmadensis. The first part names the group, the second the species. Within the rules, the scientists can choose almost anything: a description, a place, a person or even a joke.

st.prompt: Two scientists give the same dinosaur two different names. Which name does the world use?

options.t: The one that was published first
The one chosen by the bigger museum

st.reveal: The rule is called priority. The first name properly published wins, however good the second one sounds. That is why the name Brontosaurus was dropped for most of the 1900s.

sec.t:
The first dinosaur ever named was Megalosaurus, "great lizard", described by William Buckland in England in 1824. Back then, nobody had a word for the whole group. In 1842, the British anatomist Richard Owen grouped a few giant fossil [[reptile|reptiles]] together and called them Dinosauria. It meant "terrible lizards", in the sense of fearfully great.

That makes the word younger than India's first dinosaur find. Bones were dug up near Jabalpur in 1828, fourteen years before there was a word for them.

Names are usually built from ancient Greek or [[@latin-roots|Latin]] words, which scientists all over the world can share. [[@triceratops-horns|Triceratops]] means "three-horned face". [[@velociraptor-real|Velociraptor]] means "swift thief". The rule book is the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, which covers every animal, from ants to whales.

The name-bearing fossil, called the holotype, is kept in a museum or university so that anyone can study it later. When someone digs up a similar skeleton, they compare it with the holotype to decide whether they have the same species or a new one. A name with no holotype behind it is like a label stuck on an empty box.

The code's most important rule is priority. If two people name the same animal, the first published name wins. During the [[@bone-wars|Bone Wars]] of the 1870s and 1880s, two rival Americans rushed out so many names that some animals were named twice. One of those duplicates caused the most famous naming muddle of all.

{{story:names-meaning}}

In 1877, Othniel Marsh named a long-necked dinosaur Apatosaurus. Two years later he named a bigger skeleton Brontosaurus, "thunder lizard". In 1903, another scientist decided they were the same kind of animal. Apatosaurus was published first, so Brontosaurus was officially dropped.

The public kept the name anyway. It appeared in films, books and even on a US postage stamp in 1989. Then, in 2015, a team compared dozens of long-necked skeletons in detail. They argued that Brontosaurus was different enough to be its own genus again. After more than a century, the thunder lizard was back.

Many names celebrate where a dinosaur was found. [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]] narmadensis, "royal lizard from the Narmada", was named in 2003 from bones found in Gujarat. [[@barapasaurus|Barapasaurus]] tagorei, "big-leg lizard", honours the poet Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]]. It was dug up around his birth centenary.

Scientists try not to name dinosaurs after themselves, which is seen as bad manners. Naming one after a colleague or a hero is fine.

Some names have stories behind them. Irritator, a fish-eating dinosaur from Brazil, got its name because fossil dealers had stuck extra plaster on its skull to make it look longer. Removing it irritated the scientists. Dracorex hogwartsia, "dragon king of Hogwarts", was named in 2006. Its skull belongs to the Children's Museum of Indianapolis, and young visitors helped suggest the name. And one armoured dinosaur from Montana is called [[@ankylosaurus-club|Zuul]], after a monster in the film Ghostbusters.

text: The story has two parts. The first people of any kind in India were not our own [[species|species]]. Early humans, probably related to a species called *Homo erectus*, were making [[@stone-tools|stone tools]] in South India by about 1.5 million years ago.

Our own species, *Homo sapiens*, [[evolve|evolved]] in Africa and spread out much later. Most genetic studies suggest modern humans reached India roughly 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, travelling along the coasts of Arabia and Iran. Some [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] think they may have arrived earlier, perhaps before 74,000 years ago. This is still debated. Either way, people lived in India for tens of thousands of years before the first villages and cities appeared.

sec.t:
At Attirampakkam, about 60 km from Chennai, archaeologists led by Shanti Pappu dug through layers of river clay and gravel. They found teardrop-shaped stone hand [[axis|axes]] and cleavers. In 2011, they reported that the oldest tools there were about 1.5 million years old.

That makes them some of the oldest hand axes found outside Africa. Whoever made them had walked a very long way. No bones of the toolmakers have been found at the site, so we don't know exactly which human species they were.

In 2018, the same team reported smaller, more carefully shaped tools from the site, about 385,000 years old. They suggested that new ways of making tools appeared in India earlier than many had believed.

{{story:stone-tools}}

In 1982, a [[geologist|geologist]] named Arun Sonakia found part of a fossil skull in the banks of the [[@narmada|Narmada]] at Hathnora, in Madhya Pradesh. It's still the oldest human [[fossil|fossil]] found in India.

Experts have argued about it ever since. Some thought it belonged to *Homo erectus*. Others see features closer to later humans. Estimates of its age range widely, from around 250,000 years to much younger. It's a reminder that India's early human story has big gaps that future finds may fill.

About 74,000 years ago, the Toba [[@volcano|volcano]] in Sumatra erupted with enormous force. A layer of its ash settled over much of India and can still be found in the ground today.

At Jwalapuram, in Andhra Pradesh, archaeologists found stone tools both below and above this ash. Some argued that the tools below it were made by modern humans, which would mean our species arrived before 74,000 years ago. Others think those tools were made by earlier human species, which would fit with genetic studies pointing to a later arrival.

At Bhimbetka, in the forests of Madhya Pradesh, hundreds of rock shelters were lived in for tens of thousands of years. Their walls carry paintings of hunters, dancers, deer, bison and elephants in red and white. Some are thought to be around 10,000 years old or older, though dating rock art is difficult. Bhimbetka became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003, and it holds some of the oldest known [[@cave-art|cave paintings]] in India.

[[dna|DNA]] studies show that almost everyone in India today carries ancestry from those first modern humans. Later, other groups arrived too, including early farmers from the region of Iran and herders from Central Asia, and their ancestries mixed over thousands of years.

So India's population is a blend of very old and newer roots. Scientists study this mixing by comparing DNA from living people with DNA from ancient skeletons, including one woman buried at the Indus city of Rakhigarhi about 4,500 years ago. Long before the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] were built, hunters and gatherers had already learned India's rivers, forests and seasons.

text: परी-घेरे नंगी ज़मीन के गोल टुकड़े हैं, आम तौर पर 2 से 12 मीटर चौड़े, और हर एक के चारों ओर ऊँची घास का घेरा होता है। ये दक्षिणी अफ़्रीका में नामीब रेगिस्तान के किनारे और पश्चिमी [[@australia|ऑस्ट्रेलिया]] के पिलबारा इलाके में लाखों की तादाद में मिलते हैं। हवाई जहाज़ से देखो तो ये किसी विशाल बिंदीदार कंबल जैसे लगते हैं।

कोई पूरी तरह पक्का नहीं है कि इन्हें क्या बनाता है। एक विचार यह है कि ज़मीन के नीचे रहने वाली रेत की दीमकें घास की जड़ें खा जाती हैं, जिससे एक घेरे में घास मर जाती है और मिट्टी का पानी उनके अपने लिए बच जाता है। दूसरा यह है कि घास ख़ुद यह पैटर्न बनाती है: बहुत सूखी मिट्टी में पौधे पानी के लिए होड़ करते हैं, और खाली घेरे आसपास की घास के लिए पानी के भंडार का काम करते हैं। वैज्ञानिक अब भी दोनों के लिए सबूत जुटा रहे हैं।

sec.t:
नामीबिया में परी-घेरे रेगिस्तान और घास के मैदानों के बीच लगभग 2,000 किलोमीटर लंबी पट्टी में फैले हैं। इनके बीच की दूरी हैरानी की हद तक एक जैसी है, हर घेरा अपने पड़ोसियों से लगभग बराबर दूर, जैसे मधुमक्खी के छत्ते के खाने। यह नियमित दूरी इस बात का सबसे अच्छा सुराग है कि ये बनते कैसे हैं।

घेरे बनते हैं, बढ़ते हैं और धीरे-धीरे फिर भर जाते हैं। एक अध्ययन का अनुमान है कि एक आम घेरा लगभग 40 साल चलता है, और बड़े घेरे शायद इससे कहीं ज़्यादा। वहाँ की लोक-कथाएँ कहती हैं कि ये देवताओं के पैरों के निशान हैं, या वे जगहें जहाँ एक ड्रैगन ने आग उगली थी।

स्टीफ़न गेट्ज़िन समेत दूसरे वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि घास यह सब अकेले करती है। सूखी ज़मीन में घास का हर गुच्छा पानी पकड़ने के लिए जड़ें फैलाता है। जहाँ पौधे कम हैं, वहाँ वे आसपास से पानी जीतते रहते हैं, और बीच में ख़ाली जगहें छूट जाती हैं। इस तरह के पैटर्न का गणित सबसे पहले कोड तोड़ने वाले [[@alan-turing|एलन ट्यूरिंग]] ने निकाला था, जिन्होंने 1952 में दिखाया कि सीधे-सादे नियमों से क़ुदरत में धब्बे और धारियाँ कैसे बन सकते हैं।

2016 में गेट्ज़िन के दल ने ऑस्ट्रेलिया में न्यूमैन क़स्बे के पास परी-घेरों का ब्योरा दिया। वहाँ उन्हें दीमक की कोई ऐसी [[species|प्रजाति]] नहीं मिली जो नामीबिया वाले पैटर्न से मेल खाए। उनके लिए इससे साबित हुआ कि घास यह अकेले कर सकती है। दीमक पर शोध करने वालों ने जवाब दिया कि शायद ऑस्ट्रेलियाई दीमकों का भी इसमें हाथ हो।

कुछ शोधकर्ता मानते हैं कि दीमकें और पानी की होड़ मिलकर काम करती हैं। हो सकता है कुछ घेरे दीमकें शुरू करें, और पानी की होड़ उन्हें बराबर दूरी पर रखे। दोनों विचारों को मिलाने वाले कंप्यूटर मॉडल ऐसे पैटर्न बनाते हैं जो असली घेरों से काफ़ी मिलते-जुलते हैं।

2023 में उपग्रह तस्वीरों और कंप्यूटर विश्लेषण से हुए एक बड़े सर्वे में 15 देशों की सैकड़ों जगहों पर परी-घेरों जैसे पैटर्न मिलने की बात कही गई। दूसरे शोधकर्ताओं ने सवाल उठाया कि क्या ये सब असली परी-घेरे हैं। मैदानी काम मुश्किल है। घेरे दूर-दराज़, गर्म जगहों पर हैं, और प्रयोगों में सालों लगते हैं क्योंकि घेरे बहुत धीरे बदलते हैं। वैज्ञानिक खाइयाँ खोदते हैं, बारिश के बाद मिट्टी का पानी नापते हैं और दीमकें गिनते हैं, एक-एक वर्ग मीटर करके।

परी-घेरे क़ुदरत के उन बहुत-से ख़ुद-ब-ख़ुद बनने वाले [[@patterns-nature|पैटर्नों]] में से एक हैं: ज़ेबरा की धारियाँ, रेत के टीलों पर लहरें और जिराफ़ के षट्भुज। अफ़्रीका और ऑस्ट्रेलिया के कुछ हिस्सों में सूखी जगहों पर पौधों की ऐसी पट्टियाँ भी उगती हैं जिन्हें टाइगर बुश कहते हैं। बारिश, जड़ों और दीमकों के बीच कहीं इसका जवाब छिपा है। और अमेरिका के एक रेगिस्तान में वैज्ञानिकों ने एक अलग रहस्य कैमरे लगाने के बाद ही सुलझाया: ऐसी चट्टानें जो अपने-आप खिसकती लगती थीं, जिन्हें [[@mystery-sailing-stones|सेलिंग स्टोन्स]] कहते हैं।

text: [[galaxy|Galaxies]] are huge groups of stars, gas and dust held together by [[@gravity-fall|gravity]]. Sometimes two of them drift close enough for [[gravity|gravity]] to pull them together. Over hundreds of millions of years, they swing past each other, stretch out into long tails, loop back and finally settle into one bigger galaxy.

Surprisingly, the stars themselves almost never collide, because the gaps between them are enormous. What does crash together is the gas. When giant gas clouds slam into each other, they squeeze and collapse, and new stars are born in great bursts. Collisions are one of the main ways [[@galaxies|galaxies]] grow and change shape.

st.prompt: When two galaxies collide, how many of their stars crash into each other?
st.reveal: Stars are tiny compared with the gaps between them. If the Sun were a grain of sand, the nearest star would be another grain about 15 kilometres away. So two galaxies mostly pass through each other, star past star, and gravity does the real damage.

sec.t:
A galaxy collision is far too slow to watch. It takes hundreds of millions of years. But the universe contains so many galaxies that [[astronomer|astronomers]] can see collisions at every stage, like photographs from many different car crashes.

In the Antennae Galaxies, two spiral galaxies are tangled together, with two long curved tails of stars streaming out like an insect's feelers. In the Cartwheel Galaxy, a smaller galaxy punched straight through a larger one, sending a ring of new stars rippling outward. In 2022 the [[@webb-telescope|Webb]] telescope photographed the Cartwheel in sharp detail.

The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest big galaxy, about 2.5 million [[@light-years|light-years]] away. On a very dark night you can see it as a faint smudge without a telescope. It is moving towards us at about 110 kilometres per second.

In 2012, astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope predicted a head-on collision in about 4 billion years. In 2025, a team used newer measurements and included the pull of other nearby galaxies. They ran thousands of simulations and found about a 50 per cent [[@probability|chance]] of a merger within the next 10 billion years. It is a coin toss, not a certainty. A closer look at Andromeda's motion in the coming years should shrink the uncertainty.

If a merger does happen, the night sky would change slowly over many millions of years. Andromeda would grow larger and brighter, until it filled much of the sky. Then the sky would fill with streams of stars and glowing clouds of new star formation.

The two spiral galaxies would probably end up as one big, rounded galaxy, an elliptical. Astronomers sometimes jokingly call it "Milkomeda". By then the Sun will be near the end of its life, and Earth will be far too hot for life as we know it.

Most large galaxies have a giant [[@black-holes|black hole]] at their centre. When galaxies merge, their black holes sink towards the middle, circle each other and eventually join. As they spiral together, they send out ripples in space called gravitational waves. Scientists are building new instruments to detect the biggest of these mergers across the universe.

text: Manta rays are [[filter-feeder|filter feeders]]. They eat [[plankton|plankton]]: tiny shrimp-like animals, fish eggs and [[larva|larvae]] drifting in the water. A manta swims with its huge mouth wide open, scooping up water like a moving net. Two flaps on either side of its head, called cephalic fins, unroll to funnel water and food into its mouth.

Inside, the water flows out through the gills, but the food is caught by filter plates and swallowed. Because plankton is tiny, a manta has to filter enormous amounts of water to get enough to eat. The giant oceanic manta, the biggest kind, can measure about 7 m from wingtip to wingtip, about as wide as a minibus is long. Yet it never bites prey.

sec.t:
When you sieve something, the holes often get blocked. Mantas seem to avoid that. In 2018, scientists in California studied the filter plates of manta rays and built models of them. They found that food particles bounce, or ricochet, off the plates and stay in the mouth, while water flows out through the gaps.

This trick lets mantas catch bits of food even smaller than the gaps in their filter, without getting clogged. Engineers are now interested in copying the idea for [[@water-purify|water filters]]. The biggest animal on Earth, the [[@blue-whale|blue whale]], is also a filter feeder, though it uses comb-like plates of baleen instead.

Manta rays have large brains for fish, with especially big areas linked to learning. Some scientists think they may be among the smartest fish, though testing intelligence in a fish is hard. They also visit cleaning stations on [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]], where small fish nibble off [[parasite|parasites]] and dead skin, and they seem to remember where these stations are.

Each manta has a unique pattern of dark spots on its white belly. Like human [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]], no two are the same. Divers photograph these spots and share them with scientists, who use them to recognise and track individual mantas over many years.

Mantas and their relatives are cartilaginous fish, like [[@sharks-old|sharks]]: their skeletons are made of bendy [[cartilage|cartilage]], not bone. Unlike many stingrays, they have no sting. Their name comes from the Spanish word for a cloak or blanket.

Mantas grow slowly and usually have just one pup every two years or more, so their numbers recover slowly. They are [[@fishing-sustainable|caught in fishing nets]] and hunted for their gill plates, which are sold for use in some traditional remedies. In 2018, the USA listed the giant oceanic manta as a threatened [[species|species]]. International trade in mantas is controlled, and many countries, including the Maldives, protect them.

text: Many [[atom|atoms]] act like teeny magnets, because of the way their tiny [[electron|electrons]] spin and move. In most materials, these atomic magnets point every which way and cancel out.

In iron, the tiny magnets can line up in the same direction, so the whole thing becomes magnetic. Nickel and cobalt can do this too, and so can a few rarer metals. Gold, [[@aluminium|aluminium]], copper and silver can't, so a magnet ignores them.
Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why a compass works.

sec.t:
Inside a piece of iron, atoms form small groups called *domains*. In each domain, millions of atomic magnets point the same way. In an ordinary iron nail, the domains point in different directions, so the nail isn't a magnet on its own.

Bring a magnet close, and the domains swing round to line up with it. Now the nail is a magnet too, and it's pulled in. Take the magnet away and most domains drift back, which is why a paperclip only stays magnetic for a short while. In a permanent magnet, the domains stay lined up.

Heat jiggles atoms about. Get iron hotter than about 770°C and the domains fall apart, so the magnetism vanishes.

Every magnet has two ends, called poles: north and south. Opposite poles pull together and matching poles push apart. Try pushing two north poles together and you can feel the invisible cushion between them.

Snap a magnet in half and you don't get a lone north and a lone south. You get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

Compasses work because [[@earth-magnet|Earth]] behaves like a giant magnet. Its outer core is liquid iron, swirling as the planet turns, and that moving metal makes a magnetic field. The field also shields us from harmful particles streaming from the Sun.

Some animals sense this field. Young [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] seem to use it to find their way across whole oceans, and many birds use it on long [[@migration|migrations]].

Magnets and electricity are two sides of the same force. Run a current through a coil of wire and it becomes a magnet, called an electromagnet. Scrapyard cranes use giant ones to lift cars, then switch them off to drop them.

The reverse works too. Moving a magnet near a wire makes [[@electricity-made|electricity]] flow. Every power station, every electric motor and every speaker uses this link.

The strongest everyday magnets, made with a metal called neodymium, were invented in the 1980s. A small one can lift many times its own weight, and they hide inside phones, [[@how-headphones|earbuds]] and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]].

Big magnets can even lift trains. [[@maglev|Maglev]] trains float just above the track, held up and pushed along by magnets, so there's no wheel rubbing on rail. The Shanghai maglev in China has carried passengers at around 430 km/h.

इनमें कृष्ण और राधा हैं, रामायण के दृश्य हैं, शिकार पर निकले राजा हैं, छज्जों पर बैठी स्त्रियाँ हैं, और संगीत के टुकड़े तक हैं। बहुत से चित्रों को लघुचित्र कहते हैं, क्योंकि ये इतने छोटे हैं कि हथेलियों में थामे जा सकें। देखने वाले इन्हें पास से, आराम से देखते थे, हाथों-हाथ आगे बढ़ाते थे और उनमें दिखाई कहानी या संगीत पर बातें करते थे।

sec.t:
कला इतिहासकार राजपूत चित्रकला को दो मुख्य समूहों में बाँटते हैं। राजस्थानी चित्रकला मैदानों के दरबारों से आई, जैसे मेवाड़ (उदयपुर), बूँदी, कोटा, किशनगढ़, जयपुर और बीकानेर। पहाड़ी चित्रकला, यानी "पहाड़ों की", हिमालय की तलहटी की छोटी रियासतों से आई, जैसे बसोहली, गुलेर और [[@kangra-painting|काँगड़ा]]।

हर दरबार की अपनी शैली थी। मेवाड़ के चित्र दमदार हैं, उनकी पृष्ठभूमि सपाट लाल और पीली होती है। कोटा के कलाकारों को घने जंगल में जंगली शिकार के दृश्य बहुत भाते थे। बसोहली के चित्रों में तीखे रंग हैं, और पन्ने जैसा दिखाने के लिए उनमें चमकीले भृंग के पंखों के टुकड़े तक चिपकाए गए हैं। काँगड़ा के चित्र ज़्यादा नरम और नाज़ुक हैं, हल्के हरे रंगों और कोमल चेहरों वाले।

चित्रकार हाथ से बने कागज़ से शुरुआत करते थे। मज़बूती के लिए अक्सर कई परतें आपस में चिपका दी जाती थीं। फिर उसे चिकने पत्थर से घिसा जाता, हल्के लाल रंग से ख़ाका खींचा जाता, और परत-दर-परत रंग भरे जाते।

रंग [[mineral|खनिजों]], पौधों और दूसरी कुदरती चीज़ों को पीसकर बनते थे: लाल रंग सिंगरफ़ से, नीला नील या लाजवर्द से, सफ़ेद सीपियों से। मुकुट और गहनों के लिए असली सोने-चाँदी को कूट-कूटकर बुरादा बनाया जाता था। सबसे बारीक कूचियों में गिलहरी की पूँछ के गिने-चुने बाल होते थे। एक चित्र में हफ़्तों लग सकते थे, और अक्सर कई कलाकार एक ही चित्र पर काम करते थे, हर कोई वह हिस्सा बनाता जिसमें वह सबसे माहिर हो।

[[@mughal-miniatures|मुग़ल बादशाहों]] के बड़े-बड़े चित्रशाला थे, और बहुत से राजपूत राजा उनके दरबार में समय बिताते थे। विचार दोनों तरफ़ आए-गए। राजपूत चित्रों ने कुछ मुग़ल आदतें अपनाईं, जैसे चेहरों पर छाया देना और राजाओं के व्यक्ति-चित्र बनाना। मुग़ल चित्रकारों ने राजपूत रंग और विषय अपनाए।

फिर भी दोनों शैलियाँ अलग लगती हैं। मुग़ल चित्र अक्सर असली दृश्यों में खुलती खिड़की जैसे लगते हैं। राजपूत चित्र ज़्यादा कविता जैसे लगते हैं: गद्दियों जैसी गोल पहाड़ियाँ, नक्काशीदार फ़ीतों जैसी नदियाँ, और आसमान जो बेवजह चटक नारंगी हो सकता है, बस इसलिए कि वह बहुत सुंदर लगता है।

लगभग 1750 में किशनगढ़ के दरबार में चित्रकार निहाल चंद ने बणी-ठणी नाम से जानी जाने वाली एक स्त्री का चित्र बनाया, लंबी, कमान जैसी आँख और तीखी नाक वाला। यह छवि इतनी मशहूर हुई कि भारतीय डाक विभाग ने 1973 में इस पर डाक टिकट जारी किया। लोग कभी-कभी इसे भारत की मोनालिसा कहते हैं।

राजपूत चित्र तुम उदयपुर, जयपुर और नई दिल्ली के संग्रहालयों में देख सकते हो, और लंदन, न्यूयॉर्क और लॉस एंजेलिस के बड़े संग्रहों में भी। [[@rajasthan-forts|राजस्थान के किलों]] के कई महलों की दीवारें भी इसी शैली में रंगी हैं, जैसे बड़े-बड़े [[mural|भित्तिचित्र]]।

text: A mahout is a person who rides, trains and cares for an elephant. In India, mahouts look after elephants that belong to temples, forest departments, festivals and tourist camps. The job is old: Indian texts thousands of years old already describe elephant keepers and the hooked stick, called an ankus, they carried.

A mahout and an elephant often stay together for years, sometimes decades. The elephant learns his voice, his smell and his habits. In many families the work passes from father to son, so a boy may grow up beside the elephant he will one day guide.

A language of words and touches
sec.t:
Mahouts guide elephants with a few dozen spoken commands and touches. A press of the foot behind an ear can mean turn. A word can mean kneel, lift your foot or pick that up. Working elephants can learn to hand a fallen object back to their rider with their trunk.

Elephants are clever and remember people for years. Like all [[@elephants-india|elephants in India]], they have moods, friends and dislikes. A good mahout learns to read the flap of an ear or the swing of a tail, and to tell when his elephant would rather be left alone.

Some of the most important mahouts work for forest departments. Their trained elephants, called kumkis, help guide wild herds away from villages and fields. In Assam's flooded grasslands, forest staff ride elephants to patrol areas no jeep can reach.

At the Theppakadu elephant camp in Tamil Nadu's Mudumalai Tiger Reserve, a couple named Bomman and Bellie raised an orphaned baby elephant called Raghu. A film about them, The Elephant Whisperers, won an [[@oscars|Oscar]] in 2023. It was the first Indian production to win that award for a documentary.

In Kerala, elephants carry golden headdresses and deities at temple festivals, most famously at [[@india-wonder-thrissur-pooram|Thrissur Pooram]]. Each elephant walks with its mahout close by, and the crowd of drums and fireworks tests both of them.

America had its own famous elephant keeper. In 1882 the giant elephant Jumbo was shipped from London Zoo to a travelling [[@circus|circus]] in the USA, and his keeper, Matthew Scott, went with him. Jumbo was so famous that his name became the everyday English word for anything enormous.

The work is changing. Animal welfare groups worry about elephants kept in chains, made to stand on hot roads, or trained with harsh methods. Some mahouts are poorly paid and badly trained, and some elephants are overworked. In 2023 a temple in Kerala began using a life-sized mechanical elephant for its [[ritual|rituals]] instead of a real one.

Others argue that skilled mahouts are needed more than ever, to care for captive elephants and to help wild ones. Either way, an elephant's memory makes the mahout's job personal. Elephants also do something even stranger with sound, which explains how [[@elephants-talk|they talk across kilometres]] of forest.

text: A religion is a set of beliefs and practices about God or gods, the meaning of life, how to live well and what happens after death. Billions of people follow a religion, and many others are not religious at all.

By most counts, the largest religions are Christianity, with about 2.3 billion followers, and Islam, with about 2 billion. Hinduism comes next, with about 1.2 billion, followed by Buddhism. About 1.9 billion people say they have no religion. Smaller faiths include Sikhism, Judaism, Jainism, the Bahá'í faith and Zoroastrianism, along with many local and traditional religions.

sec.t:
Hinduism has no single founder. It grew over thousands of years from many traditions, texts and gods, and its followers worship in many ways. Its sacred texts include the Vedas, the Upanishads and [[@bhagavad-gita|the Bhagavad Gita]].

Around 2,500 years ago, two teachers in what is now [[@bihar-history|Bihar]] founded new paths. Siddhartha Gautama, who became the [[@buddha|Buddha]], taught a way to end suffering through wisdom and kindness. [[@mahavira|Mahavira]], the great teacher of Jainism, taught strict non-violence towards every living thing. Buddhism later spread across Asia, to [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], China, Japan and beyond.

{{story:buddha}}

In the 1400s and 1500s, [[@guru-nanak|Guru Nanak]] founded Sikhism in Punjab. Sikhs believe in one God, equality of all people and service to others.

Judaism, Christianity and Islam are sometimes called Abrahamic religions, because all three honour Abraham as an early prophet. Judaism is the oldest of the three. Christianity grew from the teachings of Jesus about 2,000 years ago. Islam began in Arabia in the 600s CE with the Prophet Muhammad, and its holy book is [[@quran-intro|the Quran]].

Followers of these faiths reached India very early. Jewish communities lived in [[@kerala|Kerala]] for many centuries, and Kochi's Paradesi Synagogue was built in 1568. Christian tradition holds that the apostle Thomas came to Kerala in the first century. Historians debate this, but Christians have certainly lived there for well over a thousand years. Zoroastrians from [[@ancient-persia|Persia]], known in India as Parsis, settled in Gujarat more than a thousand years ago.

Many religions have sacred places that draw pilgrims from far away. Hindus travel to [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] on the Ganga, and Muslims who are able make the [[@mecca-hajj|Hajj]] to Mecca. Sikhs visit the Golden Temple in Amritsar, and Buddhists go to Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have found enlightenment. Christians visit [[@jerusalem|Jerusalem]], Bethlehem and Rome.

India is home to most of the world's Hindus. At the 2011 [[census|census]], about 80% of Indians were Hindu, 14% Muslim, 2% Christian and nearly 2% Sikh, with smaller numbers of Buddhists, Jains and others. In the United States, about six in ten adults describe themselves as Christian, and a growing share say they have no religion.

Religions differ in their beliefs about God and the afterlife, and their followers sometimes disagree strongly. But many share ideas about kindness, honesty, [[@charity|giving to others]] and caring for the poor. Many also mark the year with [[@festivals-unity|festivals of light]] and feasting, like [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]], Christmas, Eid and Hanukkah. Poets such as [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]] sang about faith in everyday language that ordinary people could understand.

India's Constitution protects the freedom to follow, practise and spread any religion, or none. Learning what your neighbours believe, and why, is often the first step to understanding them.

text: Vedic maths is a set of [[@maths-shortcuts-indian|mental calculation tricks]] described in a book called Vedic Mathematics, published in 1965. Its author, Bharati Krishna Tirtha, was a Hindu religious leader and scholar who was also trained in mathematics. The book gives 16 short rules, called sutras, for doing sums quickly in your head, such as multiplying large numbers or finding squares.

The tricks are real and often clever. Many schools and tuition classes in India and abroad teach them. But the name causes debate, because the rules do not appear in the ancient Vedas. India does have a long and genuine history of mathematics, from early [[geometry|geometry]] to zero, so the two are worth telling apart.

st.prompt: Using the Vedic maths trick for numbers ending in 5, what is 45 × 45?
st.reveal: Take the first digit, 4, and multiply it by the next number up, 5, to get 20. Then write 25 after it. So 45 × 45 = 2,025. The trick works for any two-digit number ending in 5.

src: Tirtha B.K. (1965) Vedic Mathematics. Motilal Banarsidass.
Plofker K. (2009) Mathematics in India. Princeton University Press.
n.certNote: The calculation tricks in Vedic maths work, and many students find them useful. Whether they really come from the ancient Vedas is disputed. Historians of mathematics have found no trace of the 16 sutras in any known Vedic text.

myth: The 16 sutras of Vedic maths are written in the ancient Vedas.

No known Vedic text contains them. Bharati Krishna Tirtha said they came from an appendix of the Atharva Veda, but nobody else has found it. Most historians think he composed or put together the sutras himself in the 20th century, while the Vedas date back around 3,000 years.

sec.t:
Bharati Krishna Tirtha was born in 1884 and studied Sanskrit, [[philosophy|philosophy]], mathematics and science. In 1925 he became the Shankaracharya of the Govardhan Matha in Puri, Odisha, one of the most important religious posts in Hinduism.

He said he had rebuilt the sutras after years of study and meditation, from an appendix of the Atharva Veda. He said he wrote 16 volumes explaining them, but the [[manuscript|manuscripts]] were lost. Near the end of his life he wrote one introductory volume from memory. It was published in 1965, five years after he died.

Each sutra is a short [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] phrase. One of the best known is Ekadhikena Purvena, "by one more than the previous one". It helps with squaring numbers that end in 5. For 65 × 65, take the 6, multiply it by one more, 7, to get 42, then add 25 at the end. The answer is 4,225.

Another sutra, "all from 9 and the last from 10", makes subtracting from 1,000 easy. For 1,000 − 357, take each digit from 9, except the last, which you take from 10. That gives 6, 4 and 3, so the answer is 643.

A rule called "vertically and crosswise" multiplies two-digit numbers in one line. These are fun, and they work because of ordinary [[@algebra|algebra]]. Once children have a firm grip on their [[@multiplication-tables|times tables]], the tricks can speed things up further.

{{story:sanskrit}}

The Vedas are among the oldest religious texts in the world, composed in the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]] roughly 3,000 years ago and passed down by memory. Scholars who know them well have not found Tirtha's sutras in them. The language of the sutras also looks much later than Vedic Sanskrit.

In 1993 the Indian mathematician S. G. Dani wrote a well-known critique. He argued the tricks were useful but had nothing to do with the Vedas, and that calling them Vedic could mislead students about India's real mathematical history. Supporters reply that the tricks still help children enjoy maths, whatever their source. Even the general editor's note in the 1965 book says the sutras are not found in the known versions of the Atharva Veda.

The Vedic period did produce real mathematics. The Shulba Sutras, written roughly 2,500 to 2,800 years ago, give rules for building fire altars of exact shapes and sizes. They include a rule about the sides of right-angled triangles, the idea now often credited to Pythagoras, along with a very good approximation for the square root of 2.

Later Indian mathematicians, such as [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] and [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]], made discoveries that changed the world. Their work on [[@place-value|place value]], zero and algebra was carried by scholars to the Arab world and on to Europe. Like the [[@abacus|abacus]], Vedic maths is a useful tool for mental sums. It is a modern tool, built by a gifted scholar, and India's ancient maths has plenty of true stories of its own.

text: Manga are Japanese comics, and anime is Japanese animation. In Japan, both are enjoyed by people of all ages, not just children. Manga cover every subject you can think of: sports, cooking, history, school life, [[@robots|robots]], ghosts and even business.

Many anime series begin as popular manga. The characters often have large, expressive eyes and spiky or colourful hair, and the stories may run for hundreds of episodes. Today shows such as *Doraemon*, *[[@pokemon|Pokémon]]* and *Shin-chan* are watched by children in India, the USA and around the world.

st.reveal: Manga stories usually come out in thick weekly or monthly magazines printed on cheap paper. Black and white keeps the cost low and lets artists finish a chapter in a week. Popular stories are later collected into books.

myth: Anime is only for young children.

In Japan, anime and manga are made for every age group, from toddlers to grandparents. Some are cheerful cartoons and others are serious stories meant only for adults, so it helps to check the age rating.

sec.t:
[[@japanese-writing|Japanese writing]] is traditionally read from top to bottom and right to left. So manga open from what English readers think of as the back, and the panels on each page are read from right to left too.

When manga were first translated, publishers flipped the pictures so they read left to right. That made right-handed characters left-handed and turned signs into mirror writing. Today most translated manga keep the Japanese order, and the last page often has a note saying "Stop, you're reading the wrong way."

In 1985, the directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata helped found [[@studio-ghibli|Studio Ghibli]] in Tokyo. Its hand-drawn films, such as *My Neighbour Totoro* and [[@myths-japanese|*Spirited Away*]], are known for detailed nature, quiet moments and brave young heroes.

*Spirited Away* won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2003, the first film not in English to win that award. Ghibli artists still draw much of their work by hand, a style that goes back to the [[@cartoons-history|earliest cartoons]].

Indian children first met anime through dubbed TV shows. *[[@jungle-book|The Jungle Book]]*, a Japanese series, was shown on Doordarshan in Hindi in the 1990s. Later came *Doraemon*, about a blue robot cat from the future, and *Shin-chan*, a naughty five-year-old.

Japan and India also made a film together. *Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama* was directed by Yugo Sako with Indian artists and writers, and was released in the early 1990s. It retells the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] in anime style and has gathered many fans since.

Manga are sold in Japan in thick weekly magazines, often more than 300 pages, which readers flip through on trains and then leave behind. At its peak in the mid-1990s, *Weekly Shōnen Jump* sold over six million copies a week.

Anime now has fans across the world who learn Japanese words, draw their own manga and dress up as characters at conventions. Japan's government even calls anime and manga part of its "soft power", the way a country wins friends through culture rather than force.

text: You fart because gas builds up in your gut and has to go somewhere. Some of it is air you swallow while eating, drinking or talking. Most of the rest is made by [[bacteria|bacteria]] living in your large intestine.

These [[microbe|microbes]] feast on the bits of food your body can't break down itself, like certain fibres and sugars in beans, onions and whole grains. As they eat, they give off gas. The gas collects, moves along the gut and finally escapes. Everyone does it, from newborn babies to kings and queens.

st.reveal: Nearly all of a fart is gases with no smell at all. Nitrogen comes mostly from swallowed air. Hydrogen and carbon dioxide come from gut bacteria. The stink comes from tiny amounts of sulfur gases.

sec.t:
Every time you gulp water, chew gum or eat fast, a little air slips down with your food. Fizzy drinks add extra bubbles of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Much of this air comes back up as a [[@burps|burp]]. The part that keeps going down travels about 7 to 9 m through your intestines.

That is why the main gas in many farts is nitrogen, the same gas that makes up most of the air around you. It has no smell at all.

sec.h: A gas factory in your gut
sec.t:
Your large intestine is home to trillions of [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]]. There are roughly as many bacterial cells in you as human cells. They help you digest food, make some [[vitamin|vitamins]] and fight off harmful germs.

But they are messy eaters. Beans and many [[@pulses-dal|dals]] contain sugars called oligosaccharides. Your body has no tool to split them, so they reach the bacteria untouched. The bacteria break them down and release hydrogen and carbon dioxide. In about a third to half of people, other microbes turn some of that hydrogen into methane.

This is one reason Indian cooks add a pinch of hing, or asafoetida, to dal. It is a traditional way to reduce gas, and some studies suggest it helps a little.

{{story:digestion-gut}}

Only a tiny part of a fart, usually less than 1%, makes it stink. These are sulfur gases such as hydrogen sulfide, the "rotten egg" smell. Foods rich in sulfur, like eggs, meat, cabbage, cauliflower and garlic, can make farts smellier.

Your nose is extremely sensitive to hydrogen sulfide. It can pick up less than one part in a million in the air. So a fart can be almost all harmless gas and still clear a room.

The sound has nothing to do with your bottom cheeks clapping. It comes from the muscle ring at the end of your gut vibrating as gas squeezes through. The faster the gas and the tighter the opening, the higher the note.

In the 1890s, a French performer named Joseph Pujol became famous as Le Pétomane. He could control those muscles so well that he played tunes on stage in Paris.

Animals fart too. Termites release methane as their gut microbes digest wood. Cows produce a lot of methane, though most of it actually comes out as burps from their front end.

Herring are even stranger. Scientists recorded them releasing streams of bubbles from their bottoms at night, making a high-pitched ticking sound. The researchers think it may help shoals stay together in the dark.

In the 1960s, NASA scientists studied fart gases while planning space missions, because hydrogen and methane can burn and a spacecraft cabin is a small, closed room. Their tests helped shape early astronaut menus, and planning [[@space-food|space food]] has been a strange puzzle of its own ever since.

Farting is normal and healthy. It shows your gut microbes are busy. If someone has belly pain that won't go away, a swollen tummy, or gas along with diarrhoea for days, they should tell a parent or see a doctor.

text: तुम्हारी जीभ छोटे-छोटे उभारों से ढकी होती है, जिन्हें पैपिला कहते हैं। इनमें से बहुतों के अंदर स्वाद कलिकाएँ छिपी रहती हैं। ये कोशिकाओं के नन्हे गुच्छे हैं, कुछ-कुछ लहसुन की गाँठ जैसे आकार के। बड़े इंसान के पास कुछ हज़ार होती हैं।

चबाते समय खाना [[@gross-saliva|लार]] में मिल जाता है। खाने के रसायन घुलकर स्वाद कलिकाओं के छोटे-छोटे मुँहों में बह जाते हैं। वहाँ वे [[receptor|रिसेप्टर]] कोशिकाओं को छूते हैं, जो अलग-अलग तरह के रसायनों के लिए बनी होती हैं। रिसेप्टर [[nerve|नसों]] के रास्ते दिमाग़ तक संदेश भेजते हैं, और दिमाग़ तय करता है कि तुम मीठा, खट्टा, नमकीन, कड़वा या चटपटा-नमकीन ज़ायका चख रहे हो।
फिर ज़्यादातर बारीकियाँ नाक जोड़ती है। इसी से तुम आम और केले का फ़र्क बता पाते हो।

मीठा शक्कर के बारे में बताता है, यानी ऊर्जा। नमकीन से तुम्हें वह [[@salt|नमक]] ढूँढने में मदद मिलती है जो शरीर को चाहिए। खट्टा अक्सर कच्चे फल या ख़राब हो चुके खाने से ख़बरदार करता है। कड़वा भी चेतावनी हो सकता है, क्योंकि बहुत-से ज़हरीले पौधे कड़वे होते हैं।

पाँचवाँ स्वाद है *[[@food-science-umami|उमामी]]*, एक गाढ़ा, चटपटा-नमकीन ज़ायका। 1908 में जापानी रसायनशास्त्री किकुनाए इकेदा ने पता लगाया कि [[@seaweed-food|समुद्री शैवाल]] के शोरबे को उसका गहरा स्वाद कहाँ से मिलता है। यह ग्लूटामेट नाम का एक पदार्थ था। उन्होंने इस स्वाद को उमामी नाम दिया, जो जापानी में "लज़ीज़" के लिए शब्द से बना है। टमाटर, चीज़ और [[@mushrooms|मशरूम]] इससे भरपूर होते हैं।

मुँह स्वाद से ज़्यादा भी महसूस करता है। [[@chillies|मिर्च]] जलाती है, पुदीना ठंडा लगता है, और कोल्ड ड्रिंक चुभती-सी लगती है। ये छुअन और तापमान वाली नसें हैं, स्वाद कलिकाएँ नहीं। मिर्च का रसायन, [[capsaicin|कैप्साइसिन]], गरमी वाले सेंसरों को चकमा देकर चालू कर देता है। पुदीने का मेंथॉल ठंडक वाले सेंसरों को चकमा देता है।

आधुनिक रसायन से बहुत पहले, भारत की पारंपरिक चिकित्सा ने स्वादों को अपने ढंग से समझा। [[@ayurveda-yoga|आयुर्वेद]] छह स्वाद गिनाता है, जिन्हें *रस* कहते हैं: मधुर (मीठा), अम्ल (खट्टा), लवण (नमकीन), कटु (तीखा), तिक्त (कड़वा) और कषाय (कसैला)। कसैला वह सूखा, मुँह सिकोड़ देने वाला एहसास है जो कच्चे केले या कड़क चाय से आता है। पारंपरिक [[@thali|थाली]] अक्सर एक ही खाने में छहों रस शामिल करने की कोशिश करती है। वैज्ञानिक तीखे और कसैले को असली स्वाद नहीं गिनते, पर ज़ायकों में संतुलन का विचार बहुत पुराना है।

text: Yes. Play-Doh began as a soft putty for cleaning wallpaper. In the 1930s, many American homes were heated by coal fires that coated walls with black soot. A company in Cincinnati called Kutol Products sold a dough that you rolled across the wallpaper to lift the dirt off.

In the 1950s, homes switched to cleaner heating and washable wallpaper, and sales crashed. Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall noticed that children loved modelling with the putty. She suggested selling it as a toy and gave it the name Play-Doh. It went on sale in 1956 and has since sold billions of tubs.

sec.t:
Kutol was a small family firm run by the McVicker family. Its wallpaper cleaner was a mixture of flour, water, salt and a few other ingredients, soft enough to knead and slightly sticky. It worked well, so well that it was one of the company's best sellers.

But after the Second World War, American homes changed. Coal furnaces gave way to oil and gas, which made far less soot. New vinyl wallpaper could be wiped with a damp cloth. By the mid-1950s, Kutol was in trouble.

The first tubs, in 1956, came in one colour: off-white. A year later red, yellow and blue arrived. A children's TV host in the USA, Captain Kangaroo, began showing Play-Doh on air, and sales took off across America.

Play-Doh's smell became famous on its own. For many adults, one sniff brings back childhood, because [[@nose-smell|smell]] is closely linked to memory in the brain. In 2018, Hasbro, which owns Play-Doh, registered the scent as a trademark, so no other company can copy it.

Play-Doh soon spread far beyond America. It's now sold in dozens of countries, and children squeeze it through plastic machines that turn out spaghetti strands, burgers and wild hairdos. In 1991 the toy company Hasbro bought the brand, and it still makes Play-Doh today.

Part of its success is that you can't get it wrong. A lump can become a snake, a cup or a dinosaur, then be squashed flat and started again. Teachers use modelling dough to help young children strengthen the small muscles in their fingers, which they later need for holding a pencil. Animators use similar clays too: every second of a clay film can need a dozen or more photos, with the models moved a tiny bit between each one. Fans in the USA even celebrate 16 September as National Play-Doh Day.

The exact recipe is secret, but Play-Doh is mostly water, flour and [[@salt|salt]]. The salt helps stop mould growing, which is why the dough can sit on a shelf for months. It also makes Play-Doh taste horrible, which is useful with small children.

Play-Doh was added to America's National Toy Hall of Fame in 1998. It belongs to a long line of accidental inventions. And the strangest part? Another product chemists threw away for being too sticky turned out to be one of the strongest glues ever made, as the story of [[@accident-superglue|superglue]] shows.

text: "The cloud" means using computers that belong to someone else, over the internet. When you save a photo to the cloud, it is copied across the [[@internet-how|internet]] to a powerful computer, called a [[server|server]], in a building called a [[@data-centres|data centre]]. When you watch a film online, a server sends it to you in small pieces.

You never see these computers, so they feel like they are nowhere. That is where the name comes from. For decades, engineers drawing networks on whiteboards sketched the internet as a fluffy cloud, meaning "out there somewhere, we don't need to show the details".

The cloud is made of real computers in buildings on the ground. Your phone may use Wi-Fi or mobile signal for the first few metres or kilometres, but most of the journey is through cables, including cables under the sea.

sec.t:
A big data centre can be the size of several football fields. Inside are long rows of metal racks, each packed with servers stacked like thin pizza boxes. Cables run overhead and under the floor. Lights blink, fans roar, and it is often quite cold.

All those computers get hot, so a lot of effort goes into cooling: giant [[@air-conditioning|air conditioners]], chilled water, and sometimes cool outside air. Security is tight too. Visitors pass guards, locked doors and sometimes fingerprint scanners. Data centres also keep huge banks of [[@batteries|batteries]] and diesel generators, so that a power cut in the town doesn't switch off the servers even for a second.

The world's largest cluster of data centres is in northern Virginia, near Washington, D.C. In India, the biggest hubs are around [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] and Chennai, close to where undersea cables come ashore.

{{story:internet-how}}

The cloud's trick is keeping several copies. When you upload a photo, the company usually stores it on more than one machine, often in different buildings or even different cities. If a hard drive fails, or a flood shuts a building, your photo is still safe somewhere else.

Companies also spread their servers around the planet so data doesn't have to travel too far. Even at the speed of light, a message from Mumbai to New York and back takes a noticeable fraction of a second through the cables. For video calls and online games, that delay matters. A video you stream in Kolkata may come from a server in India, while your cousin in Chicago gets the same video from one in the United States.

Big companies don't only use the cloud to store photos. Many rent computing power by the hour. A small startup in Bengaluru can rent a thousand servers for a day to test a new app, then hand them back, without buying a single machine.

Amazon Web Services began offering this kind of rental in 2006. Microsoft, Google and others followed. Today, many apps you use, from food delivery to online classes, run on rented cloud computers. When a cloud company has a big outage, thousands of websites can stop working at the same moment.

Data centres need a lot of [[@electricity-made|electricity]], for the servers and for cooling them. The International Energy Agency estimated that data centres used about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity in 2024, and that this is rising fast as [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] grows.

Some companies build data centres in cold places like Finland to save on cooling, or next to wind and solar farms. Others reuse the waste heat to warm nearby homes. Every photo you keep forever sits on a spinning or humming machine that someone has to power and cool.

text: In 30 years, your plate may look a lot like today's: rice, roti, dal, vegetables, maybe a burger. But some of that food may be made in new ways. Meat might be grown from cells in steel tanks. Lettuce might come from a warehouse with no windows. [[protein|Protein]] might come from crickets, seaweed or [[microbe|microbes]].

The reason is simple maths. The UN expects about 9.7 billion people on Earth by 2050, nearly 1.5 billion more than today. Farming already uses about half of the planet's habitable land. To feed everyone without cutting down more forests, food will need to be grown using less land, less water and less energy.

sec.t:
In 2020, Singapore became the first country to let shops and restaurants sell meat grown from cells. A few cells were taken from a chicken and fed with [[nutrient|nutrients]] inside a tank called a bioreactor, a bit like a giant pressure cooker. They multiplied into chicken meat. In 2023, the US allowed two companies to sell [[@future-lab-meat|lab-grown chicken]] too.

It is still far more expensive than farm meat, and only small amounts have been sold. Some countries and US states have banned it. Whether it will ever be cheap enough for everyday meals is one of the big open questions.

A vertical farm grows plants in tall racks indoors, under pink and blue LED lights. The roots sit in water mixed with nutrients, not in soil. A building the size of a school gym can grow as much lettuce as many acres of fields, using far less water.

The catch is electricity. Lights and air conditioning cost a lot, and several big vertical farming companies have shut down since 2022. For now, they work best for leafy greens and herbs that grow fast and spoil quickly.

The sea is another farm we have barely used. Seaweed grows fast without fresh water, [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] or land. Fishing families in Tamil Nadu already grow seaweed on bamboo rafts in the Gulf of Mannar. The tiny alga spirulina is sold as a green powder all over India.

A Finnish company called Solar Foods grows [[bacteria|bacteria]] that feed on hydrogen, [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and a few minerals. The bacteria are dried into a yellow powder called Solein, which is mostly protein. It doesn't need sunlight, soil or rain. Space agencies have looked at the idea for long missions, because astronauts can't take a farm to Mars.

Other teams use [[@fermentation|fermentation]], the same process that turns milk into curd, to make milk proteins and egg whites without cows or hens.

Some future food is very old. India asked the UN to make 2023 the International Year of [[@millets|Millets]]. Grains like ragi, jowar and bajra grow on dry land, need little water and survive heat better than rice or wheat. Your grandparents' grandparents ate them every day.

The cheapest way to feed more people may simply be wasting less. About a third of all food grown is lost or thrown away, according to the FAO, and a whole branch of future-food science is about stopping that.

text: Homi Jehangir Bhabha was an Indian physicist who studied cosmic rays and the tiny particles inside [[atom|atoms]]. He became the founder of India's nuclear science programme. He started two great research centres, the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and what is now the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, both in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]].

He also planned how India might one day make [[@electricity-made|electricity]] from its own supplies of thorium. Outside the laboratory he was a painter, a lover of classical music and a keen collector of modern Indian art.

st.prompt: India has little uranium. Which nuclear fuel did Bhabha plan for India to use in the long run?
st.reveal: India has some of the world's largest thorium reserves, mostly in the mineral sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha. Bhabha designed a three-stage plan so that thorium could one day fuel Indian reactors. India is still working towards the final stage.

sec.t:
Bhabha was born in 1909 into a wealthy Parsi family in Bombay. His father hoped he would become an engineer and join the Tata steel company. So he went to Cambridge to study mechanical engineering. He passed with top marks, but he had fallen for physics. He wrote to his father that engineering was not his line and that physics was what he wanted to do.

At Cambridge he worked on how [[@particle-accelerators|fast-moving particles]] behave when they collide. In 1935 he worked out how [[electron|electrons]] and their mirror-image partners, positrons, scatter off each other. This is still called Bhabha scattering. With the German physicist Walter Heitler, he also explained how a single cosmic ray hitting the upper air can set off a shower of millions of particles.

After independence in 1947, Prime Minister [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]] asked Bhabha to lead India's atomic work. He became the first chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission in 1948. At Trombay, on the edge of Bombay harbour, he built a huge research campus.

There, in 1956, India switched on Apsara, the first nuclear research reactor in Asia. It made [[@accident-radioactivity|radioactive substances]] for medicine and research. Some of these have a known [[@half-life|half-life]], which makes them useful for tracing and timing.

Bhabha knew India had little uranium but plenty of thorium in its coastal sands. He designed a three-stage plan for [[@nuclear-power|nuclear power]] that would eventually run on thorium. Decades later, India is still building towards it.

Bhabha sketched and painted all his life. He chose the art for his institutes and supported young painters such as M. F. Husain. The TIFR art collection is now one of the notable collections of modern Indian art.

In 1955 he chaired the first big [[@united-nations|United Nations]] conference on peaceful uses of atomic energy, in Geneva. On 24 January 1966, the Air India plane carrying him on his way to Vienna crashed into Mont Blanc in the Alps. He was 56. A year later, the Trombay centre was renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in his memory, and his close colleague [[@vikram-sarabhai|Vikram Sarabhai]] took over his work.

text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi led India's struggle for freedom from British rule using a method he called [[satyagraha|satyagraha]], "holding firmly to truth". It meant resisting injustice without violence.

Gandhi asked people to break unfair laws openly, refuse to cooperate with the government, boycott British goods and accept arrest or beatings without hitting back. He believed that if people suffered calmly for a just cause, they would win public support and shame their rulers into changing. His campaigns drew in millions of ordinary Indians, including farmers and women, who had never joined politics before. People called him Mahatma, "great soul", and Bapu, "father". His methods later inspired [[@martin-luther-king|Martin Luther King Jr.]] and Nelson Mandela.

st.reveal: Gandhi had a first-class ticket, but a white passenger objected to sharing the carriage with an Indian. Gandhi refused to move to the van compartment and was pushed off the train. He spent a cold night in the station and later said it changed the course of his life.

sec.t:
Gandhi was born in 1869 in Porbandar, a small town on the coast of Gujarat. He grew up among Hindus, Jains and Muslims, and learned early about [[ahimsa|ahimsa]], not harming living things, from the Jain tradition of [[@mahavira|Mahavira]].

He was a shy student. In 1888 he sailed to London to study law. Back in India, he was so nervous in his first court case that he could not speak and sat down. In 1893, he took a job with an Indian firm in [[@south-africa|South Africa]].

sec.h: The spinning wheel and the march
sec.t:
Gandhi came home in 1915. In 1917, he helped indigo farmers in Champaran, Bihar, who were being forced to grow the crop. It was his first big campaign in India.

He asked Indians to stop buying British cloth and spin their own thread on a charkha, a spinning wheel, to make [[@khadi|khadi]]. Spinning became a daily act of protest. In 1930 he led the Salt March to the sea at Dandi to defy the British salt law. In 1942 he called on the British to "[[@quit-india|Quit India]]".

Gandhi often used fasting as a protest, refusing food to put pressure on opponents or to stop violence among his own people. In all, he spent years of his life in prison in South Africa and India.

He also had critics. B.R. Ambedkar thought Gandhi did too little to end caste discrimination, and the two clashed in 1932 over separate electorates for Dalits. Historians have criticised some of his early comments about Black Africans in South Africa. Revolutionaries thought his non-violence was too slow.

India became free on 15 August 1947, but [[@partition|Partition]] brought terrible violence between Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs. Gandhi did not celebrate. He was in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], fasting and praying for peace.

On 30 January 1948, on his way to a prayer meeting in Delhi, he was shot dead by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu extremist who opposed his efforts for Hindu–Muslim unity. His birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, and the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] marks it as the International Day of Non-Violence.

text: India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853, from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, about 34 km away. It had 14 carriages and around 400 invited guests. Three steam engines pulled it, and the journey took about 1 hour and 15 minutes.

The day was declared a public holiday. Crowds lined the tracks and climbed onto rooftops to watch. A band played and guns fired a salute as the train left. For many onlookers, it was the first time they had seen any machine move by itself.

st.prompt: How long did India's first train take to travel about 34 km?
st.reveal: The train averaged under 30 km/h, about as fast as a quick cyclist. It stopped at Sion to take on water. Today, a fast Mumbai local covers a similar distance in under an hour, with many stops on the way.

sec.t:
The Great Indian Peninsula Railway company had bigger plans. It wanted to cross the steep Western Ghats and link Bombay to the cotton fields of the Deccan. Bombay to Thane was a short, flat first stretch to test the idea.

Building on from Thane was hard. The line had to climb the Bhor and Thal Ghats. Workers cut tunnels and built zigzag tracks called reversing stations. Thousands of labourers worked with hand tools, and many died of disease and accidents along the way.

When the Bhor Ghat section opened in 1863, trains could finally climb from the coast to the Deccan plateau, near Pune. Extra engines were added at the back to push heavy trains up the steep slope, a practice that continued on this route for well over a century. Rail lines soon linked Bombay with Calcutta, and in 1870 a traveller could cross India by train from coast to coast.

sec.h: Not the first train of all
sec.t:
Trains had run in India before 1853, just not for passengers. In 1837, a small railway near Madras carried [[granite|granite]] for building roads. In 1851, a steam engine called Thomason hauled earth and building material at Roorkee, where engineers were building the Ganga Canal.

So the Bombay to Thane train was India's first passenger train, not its first train. The first passenger train in eastern India ran from Howrah to Hooghly in August 1854.

Lines spread fast across British India. They carried cotton to the ports, soldiers to the borders, and pilgrims to holy places. Indians began travelling far from home as never before, and the railway helped people from different regions meet, trade and organise, including during the freedom movement.

Today, [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]] runs about 69,000 km of route (2024), enough to wrap around the Earth more than one and a half times. It carries close to 2 crore passengers a day and employs over 12 lakh people, one of the biggest workforces of any organisation on Earth.

The station where the first train began, Bori Bunder, was rebuilt as a huge Gothic building, now Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Mumbai's [[@india-wonder-mumbai-local|local trains]] still run along the original route to Thane every few minutes. The old steam engines are long gone, and trains like the [[@vande-bharat|Vande Bharat]] can now reach 160 km/h on some lines, more than five times faster than Sahib, Sindh and Sultan.

text: The statues on Easter Island, called moai, were carved by the Rapa Nui, the Polynesian people of the island. Their ancestors sailed across the Pacific Ocean in large canoes and settled the island, probably around 1200 CE.

Over the next few hundred years, they carved about 900 moai from volcanic rock. Most were placed on stone platforms near the coast, facing inland, with their backs to the sea. They are thought to represent important ancestors, watching over the villages and their people. The island is tiny, only about 160 square kilometres, and it is one of the most remote places on Earth where people live.

st.prompt: Almost all of Easter Island's statues were carved in one place. Where?

options.t: In the crater of an old volcano called Rano Raraku
From boulders scattered along the beaches
On another island, then brought by canoe

st.reveal: Rano Raraku is made of tuff, a soft volcanic rock formed from packed ash. Hundreds of statues are still there, some half-carved and still attached to the rock face.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rapa Nui National Park.
Hunt T. and Lipo C. (2011) The Statues That Walked. Free Press.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Easter Island.
n.certNote: Experts agree that the Rapa Nui people carved the statues. They disagree about how they were moved and about why the island's population fell, which some blame on the islanders cutting down their trees and others on rats, disease and slave raids after Europeans arrived.

d.try: Stand a tall, empty plastic bottle on the floor. Tie two strings around its neck and, with a friend on each side, gently pull in turn so it tips and twists forward. With practice, the bottle "walks". That is the idea behind one theory of how the statues moved.
myth: The Easter Island statues are only giant heads.
Most statues have full bodies with arms, carved down to the hips. Many of the famous ones on the slopes of the quarry are buried up to their shoulders in soil that washed down over the centuries.

sec.t:
Polynesians were some of the greatest navigators in history. Without compasses or maps, they read the stars, the swell of the waves, the flight of seabirds and the shapes of clouds to find islands across thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

Easter Island lies about 3,500 km off the coast of Chile and about 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island. Finding it at all was an achievement.

The statues had to travel up to about 18 km from the quarry to the coast. Rapa Nui legends say the moai walked there with the help of spiritual power, called mana.

In 2012, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo, with others, tested an idea. They built a 4-tonne concrete copy and tied ropes to its head. Teams pulling from either side rocked it forward, step by step, and it really did "walk". Other researchers think the statues were dragged lying down on wooden sledges. The debate is not settled, but the walking idea fits the statues' shape and the old stories surprisingly well.

When Dutch sailors arrived on Easter Sunday in 1722, giving the island its European name, the palm forests were mostly gone. For years, a popular explanation was that the islanders cut down all their trees, causing war and collapse.

More recent research tells a more complicated story. Rats that arrived with the first settlers probably ate many palm seeds. The worst disasters came after Europeans arrived. In 1862, slave raiders took around 1,500 islanders to [[@peru|Peru]], and diseases followed. By 1877, only about a hundred Rapa Nui were left on the island.

Easter Island became part of Chile in 1888. Today about 7,700 people live there, many of them Rapa Nui, who keep their language, dances and festivals alive. The island is a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

The islanders also had a script called rongorongo, carved on wooden tablets. No one can read it today, and it is one of the few [[@writing-began|writing systems]] still undeciphered.

text: The Rann of Kutch is a vast salt marsh in Gujarat, near India's border with Pakistan. It has two parts: the Great Rann in the north, about 7,500 square km by a common estimate, and the smaller Little Rann to the south-east. The word *rann* comes from an old word for a salty, swampy place.

For a few months after the [[monsoon|monsoon]], much of it lies under shallow water. Then the sun bakes it dry, and the salt that was [[dissolve|dissolved]] in the water is left behind as a white crust. In winter, on a full-moon night, the Great Rann glows almost silver. It is one of the strangest landscapes in Asia.

st.prompt: In the dry season, the Great Rann is a crust of white salt. What does much of it turn into during the monsoon?

options.t: A shallow, muddy lake that joins the sea

st.reveal: Monsoon rain and high sea tides flood the low, flat land, leaving water only knee-deep or less over huge areas. When it dries in the winter sun, the salt left behind forms the white crust visitors come to see.

src: Gujarat Forest Department, Wild Ass Sanctuary, Little Rann of Kutch.

d.try: Dissolve two spoonfuls of salt in a cup of warm water. Pour a thin layer into a dark plate and leave it in a sunny window for a few days. As the water evaporates, watch the white crust form, just like a tiny Rann.
myth: The Rann of Kutch is a sandy desert, like the Thar.
It is a seasonal salt marsh. It floods in the monsoon and dries into a hard, flat layer of salt and clay, with very little sand. Grassy patches and islands of higher ground dot its edges.

sec.t:
The Little Rann is home to the Indian wild ass, a fast, tough relative of the horse with a sandy coat and a dark stripe along its back. In the 1960s, only a few hundred were left. A [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] was set up in 1972, and a 2024 count found about 7,600.

When the Great Rann floods, it becomes a nursery for birds. Tens of thousands of greater [[@flamingos-pink|flamingos]] gather in some years to nest on mud flats, at a spot nicknamed "Flamingo City". Cranes, pelicans and other water birds visit too. Wolves, foxes and desert cats hunt around the edges.

sec.h: Salt farmers of the Little Rann
sec.t:
Gujarat produces about three-quarters of India's [[@salt|salt]], and a lot of it comes from the edges of the Little Rann. Families called Agariyas spend the dry months there, pumping up salty water from under the ground into flat pans. The sun does the rest, drying it into crystals.

The work is hard. Temperatures go above 45 °C in summer, and the white salt reflects the glare. Agariyas have done this for generations, living in simple shelters out on the flats until the rains return and wash the pans away. It is a lot like the [[@salt-pans|salt pans]] on coasts, only far from the sea.

On an island of higher ground in the Great Rann lies Dholavira, one of the largest cities of the [[@indus-cities|Indus civilisation]]. It was busy around 4,500 years ago. Its builders cut stone [[reservoir|reservoirs]] and channels to catch every drop of rain, because fresh water was precious even then.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] found a row of ten large Indus signs near one of its gates, possibly a kind of signboard, though nobody can read the script yet. In 2021, UNESCO listed Dholavira as a World Heritage Site.

Every winter, Gujarat holds the Rann Utsav, a festival near the village of Dhordo, at the edge of the white desert. Visitors stay in tents, buy [[embroidery|embroidery]], mirror-work and pottery made by local craftspeople, and walk out onto the salt at sunrise. Months later, the rain comes back, and the white plain vanishes under water again.

text: People made maps long before they had paper. The oldest known map of the whole world is a small clay tablet from Babylon, in what is now Iraq, made about 2,600 years ago. It shows Babylon in the middle, a river running through it, and a ring of salty ocean around the edge.

Early maps were drawn from what travellers remembered and what merchants said. Over time, people learned to measure angles and distances, and maps became less like stories and more like accurate pictures of the ground. Today a satellite does the looking, but the big ideas are thousands of years old.

st.prompt: How did sailors in the Marshall Islands in the Pacific map the ocean?

options.t: With frames of sticks and shells that showed the pattern of the waves
With knots tied in long ropes

st.reveal: Marshallese navigators tied palm ribs into frames. Curved sticks showed how ocean swells bend around islands, and shells marked the islands themselves. The charts were studied on land and left at home.

src: The British Museum, the Babylonian Map of the World (object 92687).
Library of Congress, the 1507 Waldseemüller world map.
Survey of India, history of the Great Trigonometrical Survey.
n.certNote: Historians agree on the Babylonian world map and Ptolemy's work. They disagree about older drawings, such as a wall painting at Çatalhöyük in Turkey, that some see as maps and others see as patterns.

myth: People in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was flat, and their maps showed it.

Greek thinkers had shown the Earth was round more than 2,000 years ago, and educated people in medieval Europe, the Islamic world and India knew it. Round-world maps were simply hard to draw on flat parchment.

sec.t:
The Babylonian tablet is not accurate, and it was never meant to be. It is a picture of how its makers saw their world: their great city at the centre, and strange far-off lands beyond the sea.

Other peoples made very different maps. In the Marshall Islands, navigators tied palm ribs and shells into stick charts that showed how ocean swells bend around islands. Many Indigenous Australian groups kept maps in songs, where each verse named the next waterhole on a long walk. A map, it turns out, is anything that helps you get from here to there.

About 2,200 years ago, a scholar named Eratosthenes, who ran the great library in Alexandria, worked out the size of the Earth. He compared the length of shadows in two Egyptian cities at noon and used simple [[@geometry-everyday|geometry]]. His answer was close to the real figure.

Around 150 CE, Claudius Ptolemy wrote a book called *Geography*. He listed thousands of places with two numbers each, much like the [[latitude|latitude]] and longitude we use now. His idea of a grid of lines over the Earth is the reason two numbers, called [[@coordinates|coordinates]], can pin down any spot.

sec.h: A map with south on top

sec.t:
In 1802, the British began the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India near [[@chennai|Chennai]]. Teams carried a huge instrument called a theodolite, weighing about half a tonne, to measure angles between hilltops. Step by step, they built a chain of triangles across the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]].

The survey took decades. In 1852, an Indian mathematician named Radhanath Sikdar, working on the survey's figures, found that a peak called Peak XV was the highest anywhere. It was later named [[@mountaineering|Mount Everest]], after a former head of the survey. The mountain became a target for climbers, which you can read about in [[@everest-first|the first climb of Everest]].

In 1507, a German mapmaker named Martin Waldseemüller printed a huge world map on 12 sheets. It was the first map to use the name "America", after the explorer Amerigo Vespucci. Only one copy survives. The Library of Congress in Washington bought it in 2003, and it is on display there.

Paper maps still matter, but most journeys now begin on a screen. [[@maps-digital|Online maps]] mix satellite photos with data from millions of phones, so they can show a traffic jam on a Mumbai flyover or a Texas highway within minutes.

text: Japan has thousands of old stories about spirits, shape-shifters and brave children. Many of the creatures are called yokai, a word for mysterious beings that can be scary, silly or helpful. There are river imps, magic foxes, long-nosed mountain spirits and even haunted umbrellas.

The best-known tales include *Momotaro*, about a boy born from a peach, and *Urashima Taro*, about a fisherman who visits a palace under the sea. Another is *The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter*, about a moon princess found in a bamboo stalk. That last one was written down about a thousand years ago and is thought to be the oldest surviving Japanese story told in prose.

st.prompt: A kappa keeps water in a dish on top of its head, which gives it its strength. How do people in the stories defeat one?

options.t: They bow, and the polite kappa bows back and spills its water
They throw salt in its face

st.reveal: Kappa are very polite. When you bow, a kappa must bow back, the water spills from the dish on its head, and it becomes weak. Good manners beat the monster.

src: Michael Dylan Foster, The Book of Yokai (University of California Press, 2015).

d.try: Invent your own yokai. Pick an ordinary object at home, like an old umbrella or a squeaky door, and give it a personality, a power and one weakness. Japanese folklore really has an umbrella spirit, a one-eyed hopping umbrella called kasa-obake. Draw yours and tell its story to someone.
myth: Yokai are all evil demons.
Yokai can be scary, silly, helpful or simply strange. Some bring good luck, like the house spirit zashiki-warashi, said to bless families. Many are closer to mischief-makers than villains.
facts: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, about 10th century

sec.t:
A kappa is a small green creature with a beak, a shell like a turtle and a dish of water on top of its head. It lives in rivers and ponds and pulls careless people into the water. The dish is its weakness. Bow to a kappa and, being well brought up, it bows back. The water spills out and it loses its strength.

Kappa love cucumbers more than anything. That's why a cucumber sushi roll in Japan is called *kappa maki*.

sec.h: A peach, a turtle and a princess
sec.t:
Momotaro was found inside a giant peach floating down a river. When he grew up, he set off to fight a gang of ogres on a faraway island, sharing his millet dumplings with a dog, a monkey and a pheasant, who joined him. The city of Okayama claims him and has his statue outside its station.

Urashima Taro saved a turtle and was rewarded with a visit to the Dragon Palace under the sea. He stayed three days. When he returned home, 300 years had passed. He opened a box he'd been told never to open, and turned into an old man.

The moon princess Kaguya-hime grew up on Earth, turned down every suitor with impossible tasks, and finally returned to the Moon. In 2013 [[@studio-ghibli|Studio Ghibli]] turned her story into a film.

In 1776 an artist named Toriyama Sekien published an illustrated catalogue of yokai, giving many of them the looks they still have today. In the 1960s the manga artist Shigeru Mizuki made them famous again with his comic *GeGeGe no Kitaro*, about a one-eyed yokai boy. His home town, Sakaiminato, now has a street lined with more than a hundred bronze yokai statues.

Tengu are mountain spirits, sometimes shown with a red face and a very long nose, sometimes with a crow's beak and wings. Japanese Buddhism also has Karura, its name for Garuda, the bird king of Indian stories. Some scholars think crow-like tengu borrowed a little from him.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], people rediscovered Amabie, a long-haired mermaid creature from an 1846 woodblock print. In the story, she rose from the sea and told people to share her picture to protect against disease. Drawings of Amabie spread online, and Japan's health ministry used her in posters.

Yokai are everywhere in [[@manga-anime|manga and anime]]. And the strangest part? Kappa and kitsune have cousins all over Asia, from shape-shifting foxes in China and Korea to the many-headed serpents in the story of [[@myths-dragons|dragons]].

text: A riddle is a puzzle made of words. It describes something in a tricky or surprising way, and you have to work out what it is. Riddles are found in almost every culture, from ancient Greek myths to [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] paheliyan told on long train journeys.

People love them because of the moment when the answer clicks. Psychologists call it "insight", the sudden "aha!" when a puzzle snaps into place. Riddles also let you test your wits against someone else's, and a clever one is fun to share with friends.

st.prompt: The Sphinx asked, "What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon and three legs in the evening?" What was the answer?
st.reveal: A baby crawls on hands and knees, an adult walks on two legs, and an old person uses a walking stick. Morning, noon and evening stand for the stages of life. In the myth, Oedipus answered correctly and the Sphinx was defeated.

src: Exeter Cathedral Library, The Exeter Book.
