myth: The Great Sphinx of Giza in Egypt asked travellers riddles.
The riddling Sphinx is from Greek myth, a winged monster near the city of Thebes in Greece. The Great Sphinx in Egypt is a much older statue and has no riddle story attached to it.
facts: the Sphinx's riddle, answered by Oedipus
the Yaksha's questions in the Mahabharata

sec.t:
In Greek myth, the Sphinx was a monster with a lion's body, a woman's head and an eagle's wings. She sat outside the city of Thebes and asked travellers a riddle. Anyone who failed was killed. The hero Oedipus solved it, and the Sphinx was defeated.

In the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], the Pandava brothers find a lake during their exile. A spirit called a yaksha guards it, and four brothers drink without answering his questions and fall dead. The eldest, Yudhishthira, answers patiently. "What is faster than the wind?" The mind. "What is the greatest wonder?" That every day people see others die, yet live as if they never will. Pleased, the yaksha brings his brothers back to life.

Riddles appear in some of the world's oldest writings. The Rigveda contains riddle hymns, and in Vedic times priests held riddle contests as part of [[ritual|rituals]]. Ancient Babylonian school tablets include riddles too.

In England, a book copied around 970 CE, now called the Exeter Book, holds about 90 riddles in Old English. One describes a bookworm that "ate words" without becoming any wiser. Many have no answers written down, and scholars still argue about some of them.

In the 1200s and 1300s, the poet Amir Khusrau, who lived in Delhi, wrote playful paheliyan and other word puzzles in Hindavi, an early form of Hindi and Urdu. Some are still recited today.

Stories love riddle contests, because they combine danger with brainpower. In J.R.R. [[@tolkien|Tolkien]]'s The Hobbit (1937), Bilbo Baggins plays a riddle game in the dark with the creature Gollum. He wins by asking, "What have I got in my pocket?" Readers still argue about whether that was fair.

In Indian folk tales, clever characters like [[@tenali-raman|Tenali Raman]] and Birbal often face riddles from kings. The riddles test whether wisdom can beat power.

Studies suggest that solving a puzzle in a sudden flash switches on reward areas in your [[@brain-works|brain]], a little like winning a game. Scientists who study "aha" moments have found that sudden solutions feel especially satisfying, and people tend to remember them well.

Riddles also teach flexible thinking. To solve "What gets wetter the more it dries?" you have to flip the usual meaning of drying. The answer is a towel. Children who enjoy riddles are practising a skill that helps in maths, science and jokes alike: looking at the same thing from a new side.

text: Tenali Raman was a poet who, by tradition, lived in the early 1500s at the court of Krishnadevaraya, king of Vijayanagara. In Telugu he is called Tenali Ramakrishna, and in Tamil, Tenali Raman. His name comes from Tenali, a town in today's Andhra Pradesh.

He is remembered for his wit. In the stories, he fools greedy priests, proud scholars, thieves and sometimes the king himself. The tales are told in Telugu, Tamil and Kannada homes, and in comics and TV shows across India.

st.prompt: In one story, thieves plan to rob Tenali's house. He tells his wife, loudly, that the family jewels are hidden in the well. What happens?

options.t: The thieves spend all night pulling up water, and his garden gets watered
The thieves find the jewels and run away
The thieves fall into the well

st.reveal: Tenali had put only stones in a box at the bottom. The thieves hauled up bucket after bucket, emptying the well onto his dry garden. By morning the plants were soaked and the thieves had nothing.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Vijayanagar.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Krishnadeva Raya.
n.certNote: Tenali Ramakrishna was a real Telugu poet. Tradition places him at the court of Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara, but some historians think he lived a little later. Most of the funny stories are folk tales.

He is remembered as one of the poets of Krishnadevaraya's court. His Telugu poem Panduranga Mahatmyam is still studied. The jester image comes mostly from folk tales and television.

sec.t:
[[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] was a powerful kingdom in southern India from the 1300s to the 1500s. Its capital, near today's [[@hampi|Hampi]] in Karnataka, was one of the largest cities in the world at the time. Travellers from Portugal and Persia wrote about its markets, temples and horses.

Krishnadevaraya, who ruled from 1509 to 1529, was a soldier and also a poet. His court was famous for writers. Later tradition speaks of eight great Telugu poets there, called the Ashtadiggajas, or "eight elephants holding up the directions". Tenali Ramakrishna is usually counted among them, though historians still argue about exactly when he lived.

His best-known poem, Panduranga Mahatmyam, is about the god Vitthala, also called Panduranga, and his temple at Pandharpur in today's Maharashtra. It is long, learned and full of wordplay. Scholars of Telugu admire it. Very few of the children who laugh at his tricks have read a line of it.

In another favourite, the goddess Kali offers Tenali a choice of two bowls: milk for wisdom or curd for wealth. He gulps down both. The goddess is annoyed, then amused.

Many of these tales are much older than Tenali. Similar tricks appear in stories of [[@akbar-birbal|Akbar and Birbal]] in the north, and in the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], where clever animals beat stronger ones. Storytellers often attach a good plot to the most famous [[trickster|trickster]] in the area. In the south, that trickster was Tenali. Because the tales were passed on by mouth for centuries, every region has its own versions, and the details change with each teller.

The stories share a pattern. Someone powerful is proud, greedy or careless, and a sharp mind sets things right without a fight. Tenali is not always kind. He tricks people who annoy him, and sometimes the joke goes too far.

That is part of the charm. He is clever and also a little naughty, which makes him easy to like. Since the 1990s, Tenali has appeared in several [[@television-invented|television]] series and animated films. A poet whose serious work is read mostly by scholars is now known to millions of children for a burnt-mouthed cat.
